summary: This document describes how an I2NSF Controller can provide IPsec flow protection for gateway-to-gateway and host-to-host scenarios. It defines three YANG modules for the NSF-facing interface, covering the IPsec databases (SPD, SAD, PAD) and IKEv2, so security associations can be configured and monitored with little administrator effort. It defines no new protocol.

eli5.summary: A central control room can set up secret tunnels between computers instead of someone doing it by hand at each one. This document defines the forms the control room fills in.

subtitle: How a central controller can set up and watch IPsec tunnels on many devices, using YANG data models instead of hand configuration.

tldr.problem: IPsec Security Associations are normally set up device by device. Software-defined networks, such as SD-WANs, want one central place to manage them, but there is no standard interface to provision and manage security associations.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines three YANG modules for the I2NSF NSF-Facing Interface. A controller uses them to configure IKEv2, the SPD and the PAD on each device (IKE case), or to write the SPD and SAD directly, keys included (IKE-less case).
tldr.outcome: A controller can establish, rekey and monitor IPsec SAs between devices with little administrator effort, over existing protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The RFC defines no new protocol.

facts.label: Mandatory transports
facts.value: SSH for NETCONF, TLS for RESTCONF

today: RFC 9061 is a Standards Track document published in July 2021. It is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Manage IPsec From One Place
sections.content:
In Software-Defined Networking (SDN), a central SDN Controller configures and manages distributed network resources. The RFC points to Software-Defined WANs (SD-WANs), which use IPsec as the underlying security protocol, and to a cloud data center use case from RFC 8192 as scenarios that want IPsec Security Associations (IPsec SAs) managed from a central point.

The I2NSF (Interface to Network Security Functions) framework of RFC 8329 defines an I2NSF Controller that manages one or more Network Security Functions (NSFs) through the NSF-Facing Interface. This document pays attention to flow-based NSFs that protect integrity and confidentiality with IPsec. They can be hosts or gateways.

Two scenarios are covered: gateway-to-gateway and host-to-host. Host-to-gateway is out of scope, because the host may not be under the controller's control and so is not configurable. The document defines three YANG modules but no new protocol. The modules can be used over NETCONF or RESTCONF.
sections.eli5: Imagine a school with many classrooms that each need a secret code for passing notes. Instead of each teacher making up codes, the office hands them out. This document is the form the office uses.

sections.title: The IKE Case and the IKE-less Case
sections.content:
The RFC 4301 IPsec architecture separates the processing that protects packets from the key management that creates SAs. That separation lets key management be centralized. The RFC builds on it with two cases.

In the IKE case, the NSF runs IKEv2 and keeps the IPsec databases: the Security Policy Database (SPD), the Security Association Database (SAD) and the Peer Authorization Database (PAD). The controller provisions the SPD, the PAD (for example IKE credentials) and the IKEv2 parameters. The NSFs then run IKEv2 themselves to establish the SAs.

In the IKE-less case, the NSF has only the IPsec databases and no IKE implementation. The controller supplies the entries for the SPD and SAD. PAD entries are not required, since there is no IKEv2 in the NSF. The controller takes over work that IKEv2 normally does:

  • Initialization Vector (IV) generation and prevention of counter resets for the same key.
  • Generation of pseudorandom keys for the SAs.
  • Creating SAs when the NSF sends a sadb-acquire notification, and rekeying them when it sends sadb-expire.
  • NAT traversal discovery and management, random SPI generation, algorithm selection, extended sequence numbers and Traffic Selectors.
sections.eli5: Either the office gives each classroom the rules and lets the teachers invent the secret codes themselves, or the office invents every code and hands it over ready to use.

sections.title: Trade-offs Between the Two Cases
sections.content:
The IKE case is easier to deploy, because gateways typically already deploy IKEv2/IPsec and hosts can easily install it. The downside is that the NSF needs more memory and computation, since each SA rekeying MAY involve a Diffie-Hellman exchange.

The IKE-less case helps resource-constrained NSFs, but shifts the complexity of creating and managing SAs to the controller. The RFC says this may cause scalability and performance issues when the number of NSFs is high, and notes mitigations such as installing policies and SAs together (proactive mode) instead of waiting for notifications (reactive mode).

On security, the RFC states that the IKE case provides better properties, mainly because the NSFs generate the session keys and not the controller.
sections.eli5: Letting each classroom invent its own codes takes more effort from the teachers. Letting the office do it makes the office busy, and if someone peeks at the office's notebook they learn every code.

sections.title: Rekeying, State Loss and NAT
sections.content:
Rekeying. In the IKE case, IKEv2 rekeys according to the SA lifetime set by the controller. In the IKE-less case the controller MUST take care of it: when an SA is about to expire it MUST create a new SA and MAY remove the old one. This starts on a sadb-expire notification or on the controller's own initiative, using lifetime state data from the NSF.

State loss. If an NSF restarts, it loses its IPsec state, and by default the controller assumes all of it is gone. In the IKE case the controller may need to resend IKEv2, SPD and PAD information, or the IKEv2 configuration can be kept in the NSF's startup configuration datastore. In the IKE-less case the controller SHOULD delete the old SAs on the non-failed nodes, and MUST take the actions needed to reestablish protected communication once the node restarts.

NAT traversal. In the IKE case, IKEv2 detects NATs, and UDP or TCP encapsulation of ESP packets is required. IPsec transport mode MUST NOT be used when NAT is required. In the IKE-less case the controller SHOULD detect NATs itself. If it has no way to know whether a host is behind a NAT, the IKE case MUST be used.

Before an NSF can operate in the system it MUST be registered in the controller, which MUST discover capabilities such as supported cryptographic suites. The registration and discovery processes are out of scope.
sections.eli5: When a classroom's code book is lost, the office has to hand out fresh codes. When a code is about to run out, the office makes the new one and gets both classrooms using it before throwing the old one away.

sections.title: The Three YANG Modules
sections.content:
The RFC defines three modules, and registers them with IANA, with the prefixes nsfikec, nsfike and nsfikels.

  • ietf-i2nsf-ikec holds only typedefs and groupings common to the other two.
  • ietf-i2nsf-ike covers the IKE case. Its top container ipsec-ike has a pad container (a list of peer identities, authentication methods and credentials), a conn-entry list (one entry per IKE connection, with IKE SA lifetimes, algorithms, SPD entries with Traffic Selectors, Child SA lifetimes and read-only state) and a read-only number-ike-sas container.
  • ietf-i2nsf-ikeless covers the IKE-less case. Its container ipsec-ikeless has an spd and a sad. SPD entries add a traffic direction and a reqid that links a policy to its SAs. Each SAD entry carries the SPI, Traffic Selector, mode, ESP encryption and integrity algorithms with keys, lifetimes and read-only replay statistics.

The IKE-less model deliberately simplifies RFC 4301: each policy or SA has one Traffic Selector instead of a list, because kernel implementations only admit one. It also defines notifications so the NSF can tell the controller about events.
sections.eli5: There are three forms. One has the parts both ways share, one is for NSFs that make their own codes, and one is for NSFs that are simply told the codes.

sections.title: Worked Examples from the Appendices
sections.content:
Appendix D walks through operations between two NSFs, A and B. In the IKE case the controller generates IKEv2 credentials, turns the policy into SPD and PAD entries and installs the IKEv2 configuration in both NSFs. If either install fails, it rolls back by deleting what was installed. Afterwards the NSFs establish the IPsec SA with IKEv2.

In the IKE-less case the controller picks random SPIs, one for the inbound SA in each NSF. The value MUST NOT match any inbound SPI already in that NSF, and each SPI is used in the other NSF for the outbound SA. It generates fresh keys and installs the SAs and policies. In proactive mode it installs policies and SAs at once. In reactive mode it installs only SPD entries and waits for a sadb-acquire notification.

The rekey example installs new inbound SAs first, then the new outbound SAs, then deletes the old SAs, with rollbacks defined for failures at steps 1 and 2. If only step 3 fails, no rollback happens, since the new SAs work, and the old ones go away at their hard lifetime. Appendices A to C give XML examples of configuration and notifications.
sections.eli5: To switch to a new code, the office first teaches both classrooms the new code for listening, then for speaking, and only then tears up the old one, so nobody is ever left unable to talk.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A security association MUST exist between the controller and the NSFs to protect the keys and configuration they exchange. If encryption is mandatory for all of an NSF's traffic, its default policy MUST be to drop (DISCARD) packets, preconfigured in the startup configuration datastore together with the ALLOW policies needed to reach the controller. The controller is a likely attack target and MUST be protected accordingly.

In the IKE case, the controller MUST NOT store IKEv2 credentials after distributing them, and the NSFs MUST NOT allow reading them back (write-only). A PSK MUST be removed right after it is generated and distributed. An NSF MAY generate its own private key and export only the public key.

In the IKE-less case, the controller sends the private session keys, MUST NOT store them after distribution, and an attacker with access while keys are generated might decrypt or modify traffic. The controller-to-NSF security association MUST be at least as strong as the IPsec SAs it configures, including forward secrecy where wanted and a minimum 128-bit key strength.

NETCONF over SSH and RESTCONF over TLS are the mandatory-to-implement transports, NACM can restrict access, and key material nodes are protected with the NACM extension default-deny-all.
sections.eli5: The office must never keep a copy of the secret codes after giving them out, and the classrooms must never read them back out loud to anyone.

items.label: Acquire
items.desc: Policy matched traffic but no SA exists; the controller needs to install one.

items.label: Expire
items.desc: An SA lifetime was reached; the controller starts a rekey.

items.label: Sequence overflow
items.desc: The sequence number of an SA overflowed.

items.label: Bad SPI
items.desc: A received packet carried an SPI the NSF does not know.
